key: Therefore, for the perfect man who is unavoidably summoned to power over his fellows, there is naught like Inaction.
s: After eight refinements the world cherishes in error, the chapter turns to the ruler; Guo Xiang, on chapter 11, reads inaction not as folded hands and silence but as leaving each thing to act of itself, so that nature and life are at rest.
src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 11, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 13, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907032 (2026)

opened.locator: chapter 11 (juan 13), Guo Xiang note on 故君子不得已而臨蒞天下，莫若無為 (Giles 11.27)

evidence.words: 無為者，非拱默之謂也，直各任其自為，則性命安矣。
evidence.gloss: Inaction does not mean folding the hands and keeping silent; it is simply leaving each thing to act of itself, and then nature and life are at rest.

reason: Key verbatim (verse.js ok, Zhuangzi 11.27, at 879). Opened the chapter 11 packet (whole chapter): Guo Xiang’s note on 故君子不得已而臨蒞天下，莫若無為。無為也而後安其性命之情 says verbatim that inaction is not folded hands and silence but leaving each to act of itself, so nature and life are at rest; the reading paraphrases this without addition. Plain sense faithful to Giles 11.17 to 11.27 (the eight over-refinements the world reveres, increasing error, then the perfect man summoned to power). entry-check ok.
